native_result.query: The effect of which variable on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 to 0.0923 (while becoming insignifcant) when both SES and academic characteristics are included in analysis?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.3636  (significant) to  -0.2293 (insignificant) and effect of race on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024  (significant) to 0.0923 (insignificant) when academic characteristics are considered.
native_result.HypoB: Race (SAMPLE_RACE) is the variable whose effect on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 to 0.0923 and becomes statistically insignificant when both SES and academic characteristics are included. In a logistic model for BA completion adjusted only for SES, the race gradient (coded Hispanic=0 < Black=1 < White=2, i.e., a White advantage) is +0.5024 log-odds per category step (p<0.001): Whites are substantially more likely to complete a BA than Blacks and Hispanics of similar SES. Adding academic characteristics at secondary-school completion - the composite ASVAB ability score and percentile in class - shrinks this coefficient to +0.0923 (p=0.42), statistically indistinguishable from zero. Equivalently, with White as the reference category, the Black disadvantage (-0.86 log-odds, p<0.001, SES-adjusted) disappears (+0.09, p=0.68) and the Hispanic disadvantage (-0.71, p=0.004) attenuates to -0.27 (p=0.29). The attenuation is driven mainly by academic ability: the ASVAB composite alone reduces the race coefficient to 0.0504 (p=0.66), while class percentile alone leaves it significant (0.3477, p=0.004); VIFs <= 2.4 rule out a collinearity artifact, and the pattern holds under probit, linear probability models, and race/sex subsamples. Substantively, racial differences in BA completion in these NLS data operate through academic ability and performance rather than as a direct effect of race net of SES and academic characteristics. By contrast, family size remains a strong, significant negative predictor in every specification (-0.49 to -0.61 log-odds per member, p<1e-26; also significant as categories) and SES retains significance (0.29, p=0.01) after academic controls, so neither is the variable that drops out.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 x 8; zero missing); descriptive stats and BA completion rates overall (2.69%) and by race (White 3.54%, Black 1.33%, Hispanic 1.44%), sex (F 2.95% vs M 2.42%) and SES quintile (0.68%->3.53%). 2) Nested logistic regressions M1 (background: family size, race dummies, sex) -> M2 (+SES) -> M3 (+ASVAB composite, percentile in class), tracking coefficients and p-values. 3) Systematic specification search (127 nested logit/probit pairs, subsamples, encodings) to locate the cited coefficients: 0.5024 and 0.0923 reproduce EXACTLY (4 d.p.) as the coefficient of race (label-encoded Hispanic=0, Black=1, White=2) in logit(BA ~ race + SES) vs logit(BA ~ race + SES + ASVAB + percentile). 4) Robustness: probit (0.2021->0.0340, p=0.50) and LPM (0.0095->0.0009, p=0.67) confirm insignificance; academic controls added jointly vs separately (VIF<=2.4; ASVAB alone drives attenuation: 0.0504) ; family size modeled continuously and in categories (always strongly significant, never the answer); subsamples (White+Black, White+Hispanic, males, females) confirm loss of significance.
